Type B benching is allowed only in cohesive Type B soil, never granular [5][6].\\n2. It can be a single bench or multiple benches, each at most 4 ft high, with the overall profile inside 1:1 [6].\\n3. Benching from the figure applies to cuts 20 ft or less; at 20 ft or deeper a registered professional engineer designs it [1][6].\\n4. The step heights are drawn in the figure, and the app's word copy is not confirmed. Check the official Figure B-1 or ask your competent person before cutting benches [5][6].\\n\\nShield (trench box) rules:\\n5. If the lower part of the trench is vertical and shielded or supported, the shield must extend at least 18 inches above the top of the vertical side [1].\\n6. The slope above that vertical lower portion is 1:1 maximum in Type B [1].\\n7. Shielding or shoring designs must come from the other options in § 1926.652(b) and (c) (tabulated data or manufacturer data), and the soil must be classified under Appendix A [2][10].\\n8. Timber shoring (Appendix C) and aluminum hydraulic shoring (Appendix D) tables cover trenches up to 20 ft [8].\\n9. If only the lower part is shored and the top is sloped, the shoring members must be selected for the depth of the whole trench, measured from the top. The exception is when the slope above is flatter than 3:1 [7].\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-02-t2\",\"ms\":6890,\"usd\":0.0312,\"text\":\"OSHA's Appendix B (B-1.3) gives two Type C options for excavations 20 ft or less deep; texas follows federal OSHA, so this is the rule there. At 20 ft deep or more, sloping, benching and the protective system must be designed by a registered professional engineer (Table B-1 covers less than 20 ft).\\n\\n1. Simple slope: maximum allowable slope is 1 1/2:1 (34°), the Table B-1 value for Type C (Table B-1).\\n2. Vertically sided lower portion: the bottom must be shielded or supported, and the slope above it is at most 1 1/2:1 (B-1.3).\\n3. The shield or support must extend at least 18 inches above the top of the vertical side (B-1.3).\\n4. Type C gets no unsupported vertical foot. The 3.5 ft unsupported lower portion is Type A only [12].\\n5. Any other Type C shape must follow another § 1926.652(b) option, such as tabulated data or an engineer's design (B-1.3).\\n6. Slope it flatter than 1 1/2:1 if there are signs of distress, cutting it back at least 1/2H:1V less steep. A competent person must set the reduction when surcharge loads (stored material, equipment, traffic) are present (Appendix B (c)(3)).\\n\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-03-t2\",\"ms\":9014,\"usd\":0.0318,\"text\":\"Appendix C is read in four steps, and the table values themselves have to come from the rule's tables, not from memory (29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, App. C).\\n\\n1. Classify the soil under Appendix A first. Then pick the table: C-1.1, C-1.2 or C-1.3 for Type A, B or C in mixed oak, or C-2.1 to C-2.3 for Douglas fir [10][11].\\n2. Find your row by depth band (5 to 10, 10 to 15, 15 to 20 ft) and trench width (up to 4, 6, 9, 12, 15 ft). Your 10 ft trench sits at the top of the 5 to 10 band, so confirm which band the table puts exactly 10 ft in [11].\\n3. Where the table offers a choice, pick the crossbrace horizontal spacing yourself first. Then read crossbrace size and vertical spacing, wale size and spacing, and upright size and spacing [10].\\n4. \\\"Close\\\" means planks side by side. Tight sheeting is needed in saturated or submerged soil, and where water must be retained [4][11].\\n\\nOSHA's Type B example (13 ft deep, 5 ft wide, Table C-1.2) lists three arrangements [5]:\\n- 6 × 6 crossbraces at 6 ft horizontal and 5 ft vertical, 8 × 8 wales at 5 ft vertical, 2 × 6 uprights.\\n- 6 × 8 crossbraces at 8 ft horizontal, 10 × 10 wales at 5 ft vertical.\\n- 8 × 8 crossbraces at 10 ft horizontal, 10 × 12 wales at 5 ft vertical.\\n\\nUse that only to learn the layout, not for your 10 ft trench.\\n\\nThe tables don't apply with equipment over 20,000 lb next to the trench, stored material or structures beyond a 2 ft soil surcharge, or crossbrace vertical loads over 240 lb per foot. In those cases you need tabulated data or an engineer under 1926.652(c) [11]. The table values were not rechecked on 2026-11-20, so read the whole row in the rule itself before building from it [9].\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-04-t2\",\"ms\":9772,\"usd\":0.0317,\"text\":\"Appendix D lets you pick aluminum hydraulic shoring from tables when you have no manufacturer's data. For Type C at 8 ft deep, a waler system with sheeting is required (29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, App. D).\\n\\n1. Classify the soil first under Appendix A. Type C always needs sheeting, so use the horizontal wale tables (D-1.3 and D-1.4), not the vertical shore tables [5].\\n2. Select by trench depth and width. The tables give the cylinder size and the maximum horizontal spacing for each wale size, and vertical spacing is held at 4 ft on center [5].\\n3. Cylinders must be 2 inch (at least 18,000 lb working capacity) or 3 inch (at least 30,000 lb). The aluminum rails are 6061-T6 or equivalent [6].\\n4. Put at least three evenly spaced shores in a group. Plywood between shores only stops ravelling and is not structural [8].\\n5. The tables do not apply with equipment over 20,000 lb next to the trench, or with crossbrace vertical loads over 100 lb on a one-foot section of the cylinder [6].\\n6. They also do not apply if only the lower part of the trench is shored and the upper part is sloped, unless the slope is flatter than 3 to 1 or the members are picked for the full depth [6][8].\\n7. Install from the top. Hydraulic shores are set and pumped from the top, so nobody enters an unprotected trench [8].\\n8. Outside these limits, the system must be designed under 29 CFR 1926.652(c) with tabulated data or by an engineer [6].\\n\\nThe exact table values for 8 ft in Type C are not in the excerpts I have. Read them from Tables D-1.3 and D-1.4 in the rule, or from the manufacturer's data on site.\\n\\nRelated is a 9 ft deep, 4 ft wide Type C example in Appendix D (Example 5), but its result is cut off in the excerpt [2].\\n\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-05-t2\",\"ms\":7679,\"usd\":0.0239,\"text\":\"The advance signs on a 45 mph road go 350 ft apart (A, B and C) if the agency treats it as urban high speed, or 500 ft apart if it treats it as rural (Table 6B-1).\\n\\n1. Urban low speed is 100 ft each, which is too short for 45 mph, so it normally does not apply.\\n2. Urban high speed: A, B and C are 350 ft each. The sign order is ROAD WORK AHEAD (or UTILITY WORK AHEAD), ONE LANE ROAD AHEAD, then the Flagger sign.\\n3. Rural: A, B and C are 500 ft each.\\n4. Buffer space at 45 mph is 360 ft ahead of the work, if there is room.\\n5. Cones along the work go no more than 90 ft apart (2 times 45 mph, in feet).\\n6. Cones in the taper go about 20 ft apart in the 50 to 100 ft flagger taper.\\n7. A BE PREPARED TO STOP sign may be added between the Flagger sign and the ONE LANE ROAD sign.\\n8. On a curve or hill crest, lengthen the buffer so drivers see the taper and the back of the queue in time.\\n9. An arrow board here is caution mode only.\\n\\n- The road agency decides whether your road is urban high speed or rural. Oklahoma's edition of the MUTCD is not confirmed, so ask ODOT Traffic Engineering which edition applies. Your approved traffic control plan or permit governs.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-06-t2\",\"ms\":9456,\"usd\":0.0332,\"text\":\"At 55 mph, closing a 12 ft lane takes a merging taper of at least 660 ft, with cones no more than 55 ft apart in the taper (MUTCD Part 6, taper L = W x S at 45 mph or more) [9][1][10].\\n\\n- Taper lengths for a 12 ft offset: shifting taper at least 330 ft, shoulder taper at least 220 ft, flagger (one-lane two-way) taper 50 to 100 ft [9].\\n- Cones along the work space: no more than 110 ft apart (twice the speed limit) [10][9].\\n- Buffer space ahead of the work: 495 ft at 55 mph, kept empty of trucks, materials and spoil [4].\\n- Downstream taper: 50 to 100 ft per lane [9]. At night, cones need reflective bands and must be at least 28 inches tall [7].\\n- Cone count: 660 ft taper at 55 ft spacing is 13 cones, counting both ends.\\n- The approved traffic control plan or ARDOT permit governs; ARDOT's traffic office confirms which MUTCD edition is in force (not confirmed in the library).\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-07-t2\",\"ms\":10468,\"usd\":0.0296,\"text\":\"1. Shifting taper (no lane closed): at least L / 2, which is 160 ft.\\n2. Shoulder taper: at least L / 3, using the shoulder width as W. For a 12 ft width that is 106.7 ft.\\n3. One-lane, two-way (flagger) taper: 50 to 100 ft, not based on L.\\n4. Downstream taper at the end of the work space: 50 to 100 ft, with devices about 20 ft apart.\\n5. Channelizing devices in the taper are spaced about S ft apart, so 40 ft. That gives 9 devices over 320 ft (calc: 8 spaces plus 1).\\n6. Along the work area, devices go about 2 x S ft apart, so 80 ft.\\n7. Closing two lanes in succession: a tangent of about 2L, or 640 ft, separates the two merging tapers.\\n\\nThese are national minimums, so round up. Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern.\\n\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-08-t2\",\"ms\":7297,\"usd\":0.0268,\"text\":\"The temporary route needs a detectable barrier across the full closed width, a 60 inch route (48 inches with passing areas), and ramps 12:1 or flatter (MUTCD Part 6, Section 6C.02, 6C.03, 6M.04; Minnesota's manual and your approved plan govern if stricter).\\n\\n1. Width: keep the existing sidewalk width where practical, with 60 inches as the target.\\n2. Passing space: where 60 inches can't be held, provide a 60 by 60 inch passing space at least every 200 ft.\\n3. Minimum route: the TA-28 sidewalk detour drawing allows a 48 inch route, with a 60 inch passing area every 200 ft.\\n4. Ramp slope: 12:1 (8.33 percent) or flatter, and slip-resistant.\\n5. Ramp landing: at least 48 by 48 inches, with cross-slope 2 percent or flatter.\\n6. Surface: smooth and hard, with no abrupt grade changes.\\n7. Detectable edging along a channelized route: top at least 8 inches above the walk, bottom no more than 2 inches above it, continuous.\\n8. Pedestrian channelizing devices: hand-trailing edge 32 to 38 inches high.\\n9. Signs: SIDEWALK CLOSED CROSS HERE signs must include an audible information device.\\n10. At a temporary mid-block crosswalk, curb parking must be prohibited for at least 50 ft ahead.\\n\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-09-t2\",\"ms\":10362,\"usd\":0.0333,\"text\":\"For one-lane flagging (TA-10) at 35 mph, the one-lane two-way taper is only 50 to 100 ft; the 245 ft merging taper is for a multi-lane lane closure. This is national MUTCD, and NCDOT's adoption of the current edition is not confirmed, so ask the NCDOT traffic office which edition is in force.\\n\\n1. Advance signs, from the driver: ROAD WORK AHEAD (or UTILITY WORK AHEAD), ONE LANE ROAD AHEAD, then the Flagger sign. BE PREPARED TO STOP is optional, between the Flagger and ONE LANE ROAD signs.\\n2. Sign spacing: the national table gives urban low speed 100 ft apart and urban high speed 350 ft apart. The road agency decides which category your street is.\\n3. Taper: 50 to 100 ft in front of the work, with cones about 20 ft apart.\\n4. Buffer: if there is room, leave 250 ft empty ahead of the work (35 mph), with no equipment or materials in it.\\n5. Cones along the work: no more than 70 ft apart (2 times the speed limit in feet).\\n6. Downstream taper: 50 to 100 ft, with END ROAD WORK near the end. Both signs may be left out for short-duration work.\\n7. At night, light each flagger station. On a curve or hill crest, lengthen the buffer so the taper and the back of the line of stopped cars are seen in time.\\n\\n- The approved traffic control plan or permit governs.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-10-t2\",\"ms\":9774,\"usd\":0.0405,\"text\":\"The permit checks every air test against these limits, and a reading outside any of them means evacuate (stricter CO number first; Ohio is under federal OSHA, and the app's permit uses 25 ppm CO everywhere).\\n\\n- O2: minimum 19.5%, maximum 23.5% (1926.1202 \\\"hazardous atmosphere\\\"). [9][13]\\n- LEL: maximum 10% of the lower flammable limit. Federal OSHA's hazardous-atmosphere definition uses the same 10%. [9][13]\\n- H2S: maximum 10 ppm, an 8-hour average. OSHA's sewer-entry appendix (1910.146 App. E) alarms at 10 ppm. [11][13]\\n- CO: the app's permit uses 25 ppm. Federal OSHA allows 50 ppm and NIOSH recommends 35 ppm, so set your meter alarm at 25 ppm or lower. [13][15]\\n- Test in this order: oxygen first, then flammable gas, then toxic gases. Test at the top, middle and bottom, since gases layer. [8][17]\\n- H2S and CO are optional in the app, and a blank means not measured, never zero. Keep using your meter's own alarm. [14]\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-11-t2\",\"ms\":11561,\"usd\":0.0444,\"text\":\"Keep each canceled permit at least 1 year, and the entry supervisor named on the permit must sign it before entry begins (29 CFR 1926.1205). Georgia follows the federal construction rule, so this applies as written.\\n\\nWho signs, and when:\\n1. Before entry begins, the entry supervisor identified on the permit signs it to authorize entry (1926.1205(b)).\\n2. Before signing, the supervisor checks that all tests the permit specifies are done and all listed procedures and equipment are in place (1926.1210(b)).\\n3. The completed permit is posted at the entry portal, or made available some equally effective way, so entrants can confirm the prep is done (1926.1205(c)).\\n4. The permit may not run longer than the time needed to finish the task listed on it (1926.1205(d)).\\n\\nCancel, suspend and keep:\\n5. The entry supervisor cancels the permit when the work is done (1926.1205(e)(1)).\\n6. If a condition the permit doesn't allow comes up, the supervisor cancels it. If it is temporary and doesn't change the space or add hazards, the permit can instead be suspended, and the space must be fully reassessed before reentry (1926.1205(e)(2)-(3)).\\n7. The employer keeps each canceled permit at least 1 year, and any problems met during entry are noted on that permit (1926.1205(f)).\\n8. The program is reviewed using those canceled permits within 1 year after each entry. One yearly review can cover all entries in a 12-month period (1926.1204(n)).\\n\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-12-t2\",\"ms\":9066,\"usd\":0.0263,\"text\":\"Continuous monitoring is required during entry, with an alarm that alerts every entrant, unless you can show continuous equipment isn't commercially available or periodic checks are frequent enough (29 CFR 1926.1204(e)(2)); the app's CO limit of 25 ppm is the stricter one.\\n\\nContinuous monitoring and ventilation:\\n1. Monitor continuously where entrants are working. If periodic monitoring is used, it must be frequent enough to keep conditions acceptable (1926.1204(e)(2)).\\n2. Entrants or their representative may watch the testing, can ask for a re-test, and must get the results right away (1926.1204(e)(4) to (e)(6)).\\n3. Use continuous forced-air ventilation from a clean source, aimed at where people are working, until everyone has left (1926.1203(e)(2)(v)).\\n4. Don't enter until ventilation has eliminated any hazardous atmosphere. Open additional manholes where possible and use blowers, then re-test (1910.146 Appendix C).\\n\\nLive sewer that can't be isolated:\\n5. Do pre-entry testing as far as feasible, and monitor continuously where entrants work (1926.1204(e)(1)).\\n6. Provide an early-warning system that continuously watches for engulfment, such as flooding. It must alert entrants and attendants in time to exit safely (1926.1204(e)(1)(iii)).\\n\\nIn the app:\\n- A reading outside the limits sounds EVACUATE and blocks check-in.\\n- Check-in is also blocked when the last test is older than the permit's reminder minutes, or 20 minutes if blank.\\n- A blank H2S or CO reading means not measured, not zero.\\n\\nIf the meter alarm sounds, leave immediately. The attendant stays outside and never enters for rescue without proper equipment and training.\\n\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-13-t2\",\"ms\":11846,\"usd\":0.0387,\"text\":\"The attendant stays outside the manhole the whole entry, watches and talks to the entrants, orders them out on any stop condition, and summons rescue early (29 CFR 1926.1209).\\n\\nAttendant duties:\\n1. Stays outside until relieved by another attendant (1926.1209(d)).\\n2. Communicates with entrants to check their status and tell them to evacuate (1926.1209(e)).\\n3. Orders entrants out immediately if there is a prohibited condition, an entrant shows effects of exposure, a danger develops outside, or the attendant can't do the job safely (1926.1209(f)).\\n4. Summons rescue as soon as entrants may need help escaping (1926.1209(g)).\\n5. Warns off anyone unauthorized who approaches or enters, and tells the entrants and entry supervisor if someone enters (1926.1209(h)).\\n6. Does non-entry rescue only as the employer's rescue procedure says, and nothing that distracts from watching entrants (1926.1209(i), (j)).\\n\\nA relieved attendant may enter for rescue only if the program allows it and they are trained and equipped.\\n\\nRescue team evaluation (1926.1211(a)):\\n- Check that they can respond in a timely manner for the hazard, and that they are proficient with the tasks and equipment for this type of space.\\n- Select a team that can reach the victim in time, is equipped and proficient, and agrees to tell you immediately if it becomes unavailable.\\n- Tell them the hazards and give them access to practice rescues.\\n- For a vertical entry over 5 ft deep, OSHA's non-mandatory Appendix F asks whether the service can do rope work or elevated rescue. It also says to consider airline respirators if a rescue can't be finished in about 15-20 minutes.\\n- Appendix F says services must practice at least once every 12 months, unless they have done a real permit space rescue in that time. An off-site service that declines your site can't be relied on.\\n\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-14-t2\",\"ms\":7388,\"usd\":0.0219,\"text\":\"Your last answer ended without an offer, so here is how to enter the renewal in the app and what to do after it is in. In Nevada, the renewal is a Renewal ticket called in to USA North 811 before day 28 ends (NAC 455.165).\\n\\n1. Before day 28 ends, call USA North 811 and ask for a Renewal, with the original ticket number [1].\\n2. Walk the dig area first. If the marks are gone or unclear, ask for a Re-Mark instead [1].\\n3. Ticket only the area you can dig within 14 calendar days (NAC 455.115) [1].\\n4. In the app, open Locates (office: job page › Overview › Locates row), tap Add Dig Ticket and type the new ticket number [2].\\n5. Tap Save Ticket. Called in and Expires fill themselves, with Can dig from and Start work by counted by Nevada's rules [2].\\n6. Wait for every operator to respond before digging, even if the start time has passed [3].\\n\\nThe app alerts you 7 days, 2 days and on the day a ticket expires, and an expired ticket shows red: don't dig until it's refreshed [4].\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-15-t2\",\"ms\":7378,\"usd\":0.0222,\"text\":\"1. Ticket life: a pipeline locate ticket lasts 14 working days, counting every day that is not a Saturday, Sunday or legal holiday, unless you and the operator agree otherwise in writing (16 TAC 18.1, 18.3).\\n2. Update scope: ask for an Update (or Update and Remark) covering only the area still to be dug. Whether an update prints a new ticket number is not confirmed, so ask Texas811.\\n3. Notice time: an update goes out with a 2 business day notice. If the most recent ticket is over 30 days old, you need a new ticket.\\n4. No positive response by the start time: don't dig until you give a second notice. If there is still none after 4 hours, you may begin (16 TAC 18.4(e)-(f)).\\n5. Report the second call, and any operator that still didn't answer, to the Railroad Commission through TDRF (16 TAC 18.11(d)).\\n6. Keep the marks protected from the day you start until they are no longer needed (16 TAC 18.4(g)). In the app, enter the new ticket or date on the Locates screen. The \\\"Locate tickets expiring\\\" push notification (Settings › Push notifications) alerts foremen and office.\\n\\nI can't submit the Texas811 update for you. Call 811 or use the Texas811 portal.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-16-t2\",\"ms\":6821,\"usd\":0.0232,\"text\":\"Use angular crushed stone (Class I) for PVC sewer when the spec allows it, because it interlocks and holds the haunches with modest compaction [8].\\n\\n- Crushed stone (Class I): broken faces bite into each other, so it stays put beside the pipe and gives high side support [8].\\n- Rounded gravel and pea gravel (Class II): they roll past each other and flow into haunches easily, but can shift under load, especially when wet or vibrated [8].\\n- Rounded gravel needs more compaction to reach the same stiffness as crushed stone [8].\\n- Density matters most after grain type, and smaller rock is easier to place under the haunches [8].\\n- Choose crushed stone for PVC, HDPE or PP in sewer and storm, deep cover, wet trenches, or wherever the spec says Class I [8].\\n- Rounded or sand bedding is more common for water, gas and conduit, or where sharp stone could damage coatings or polywrap [8].\\n- Keep large angular rock off coatings, polyethylene encasement and tracer wire [8].\\n- Reno's own spec isn't in the library, so check what material it calls for. Clark County's drawings use Type II aggregate base in the pipe zone [1].\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-17-t2\",\"ms\":7847,\"usd\":0.0237,\"text\":\"Allowable make-up water per 1,000 ft of pipe is shown below in gal/hr; multiply by the hours of the test (2 hours doubles it) [8].\\n\\nAt 150 psi: 4 in 0.33, 6 in 0.50, 8 in 0.66, 10 in 0.83, 12 in 0.99, 16 in 1.32, 24 in 1.99 [8].\\n\\nAt 200 psi: 4 in 0.38, 6 in 0.57, 8 in 0.76, 10 in 0.96, 12 in 1.15, 16 in 1.53, 24 in 2.29 [8].\\n\\nAt 100 psi: 6 in 0.41, 8 in 0.54, 12 in 0.81 [8].\\n\\n- Scale by length: 2,400 ft of 8 in at 150 psi over 2 hours allows about 3.2 gal [8].\\n- For mixed sizes, work out each size separately and add them [7].\\n- This is a testing allowance, not permission to leak. Use the formula and test pressure your spec calls for [7][8].\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-18-t2\",\"ms\":8786,\"usd\":0.0241,\"text\":\"Tablet method: fill no faster than 1 ft per second, hold at least 24 hours (48 hours if the water is colder than 41 F), then confirm at least 0.2 mg/L free chlorine at every sample point (AWWA C651-14 Sec. 4.3) [5].\\n\\nTablet method details:\\n1. Glue the tablets in the top of each pipe as it is laid, using an NSF-61 adhesive, and put tablets in hydrants and branches too [5][9].\\n2. Keep the pipe clean and dry until filled, because this method can't be pre-flushed [9].\\n3. Don't use tablets if the pipe got dirty or trench water got in. Flush and switch to continuous feed [9].\\n\\nBac-T sampling after final flushing (Sec. 5.1), two sets that both pass [8]:\\n4. Option A: take the first set, then a second set at least 16 hours later.\\n5. Option B: let the flushed main sit at least 16 hours with no water use. Then take two sets at least 15 minutes apart, taps running, with no flushing first.\\n6. Where to sample: one set every 1,200 ft, one at the end of the line, and one from each branch longer than one pipe length. If trench water or a lot of dirt got in, sample about every 200 ft.\\n\\nIf a sample fails, flush and resample. If it still fails, re-chlorinate by continuous feed or slug and repeat until both sets pass. No tie-in or service until the agency releases the main [8].\\n\\nOlder specs written on the 2005 edition ask for two sets 24 hours apart. The 2023 edition was not read, so any change there is not confirmed. Ask your water agency which edition governs [8].\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-19-t2\",\"ms\":6459,\"usd\":0.0256,\"text\":\"1. Effective communication: any worker must be able to reach a supervisor by voice, radio or phone that works in the area.\\n2. Observe workers for alertness and heat symptoms. Use a supervisor watching 20 or fewer people, a mandatory buddy system, regular contact with anyone working alone, or another effective method.\\n3. Designate who will call 911 / emergency services.\\n4. Remind everyone throughout the shift to drink water.\\n5. Hold pre-shift meetings on these procedures and the right to a cool-down rest.\\n6. Closely watch new workers for their first 14 days, and everyone during a heat wave.\\n\\n- The extra 10-minute cool-down every 2 hours at 95 F is for agriculture only, not construction.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-20-t2\",\"ms\":12296,\"usd\":0.0486,\"text\":\"Appendix D (29 CFR 1926 Subpart P) sizes aluminum hydraulic shoring by soil type, trench depth and width, with vertical spacing held at 4 ft on center. The library has no Tennessee-specific rule for this, so follow the stricter of Tennessee's OSHA plan and federal OSHA.\\n\\n1. Classify the soil first under Appendix A. Each table covers only one soil type.\\n2. Pick the table. D-1.1 and D-1.2 are vertical shores in Type A and B soil that needs no sheeting. D-1.3 and D-1.4 are horizontal wale systems in Type B and C soil.\\n3. Enter the table with the trench depth and width. You get the member sizes and the maximum horizontal cylinder spacing. For vertical shores, the cylinder spacing is the same as the shore spacing.\\n4. Check the cylinder ratings. A 2-inch cylinder must carry at least 18,000 lb. A 3-inch cylinder must carry at least 30,000 lb. Aluminum is 6061-T6 or equivalent.\\n5. Check the limits. The tables are not adequate with a surcharge from equipment over 20,000 lb. They are also not adequate when vertical loads on a cross brace exceed 100 lb on a 1 ft section. Those cases need an engineered design.\\n6. Examples from the appendix: Type B, 13 ft deep and 5 ft wide, uses 2-inch cylinders at 6.5 ft horizontal and 4 ft vertical (Table D-1.2). Type B with Type C traits, 18 ft deep and 12 ft wide, needs a wale with section modulus 14.0 and 3-inch cylinders at 9 ft maximum, with 3x12 sheeting (Table D-1.3).\\n\\nThe table values themselves did not come through in the excerpts. Use the full Appendix D tables or the manufacturer's data for the exact numbers.\\n\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: footnote conditions (g) that modify Tables D-1.1 to D-1.4?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-21-t2\",\"ms\":6838,\"usd\":0.0289,\"text\":\"Federal OSHA is Florida's rule for private crews, and it covers shield rules and sloping rules as below (29 CFR 1926.652).\\n\\nShield (trench box) rules:\\n1. Don't load a shield beyond what it was designed to withstand (1926.652(g)(1)(i)).\\n2. Install it so sudden lateral loads can't move it sideways or otherwise hazardously (g)(1)(ii).\\n3. Protect employees from cave-ins when they enter or exit the shielded area (g)(1)(iii).\\n4. No one is allowed inside while the shield is being installed, removed, or moved vertically (g)(1)(iv).\\n5. You may dig up to 2 ft below the bottom of the shield only if the shield is designed for the full trench depth and there is no sign of soil loss from behind or below it (g)(2).\\n\\nSloping and benching rules:\\n6. No one works on a sloped or benched face above other employees unless those below are protected from falling, rolling, or sliding material or equipment (1926.652(f)).\\n\\nSloping surcharge: the excerpts I have don't include a surcharge rule. Appendix B's Table B-1 slopes (Type A 0.75:1, Type B 1:1, Type C 1.5:1) are the maximums for excavations under 20 ft. At 20 ft or deeper, a registered professional engineer must design the sloping or benching.\\n\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-22-t2\",\"ms\":8028,\"usd\":0.0269,\"text\":\"Table 1 (29 CFR 1926.1153(c)) wants water to the blade on stationary and walk-behind saws, and (g) wants a written exposure control plan with a competent person. Illinois follows the federal rule here.\\n\\nStationary masonry saw (row i):\\n1. Use a saw with an integrated water system that feeds the blade continuously.\\n2. No respirator at 4 hours or less a shift, and none over 4 hours.\\n3. Operate and maintain it per the manufacturer's instructions to minimize dust.\\n\\nWalk-behind saw (row iv):\\n1. Use a saw with integrated water that feeds the blade continuously, maintained per the maker.\\n2. Outdoors: no respirator, at 4 hours or less or over 4 hours.\\n3. Indoors or in an enclosed area: APF 10 respirator, at any duration.\\n\\nDrivable saws (row v), outdoors only: integrated water, no respirator.\\n\\nWritten exposure control plan (1926.1153(g)):\\n1. Describe the tasks that involve silica exposure.\\n2. Describe the engineering controls, work practices and respiratory protection for each task.\\n3. Describe the housekeeping measures used to limit exposure.\\n4. Describe how you restrict access to work areas to cut the number of people exposed, including exposure from other employers.\\n5. Review and evaluate the plan at least annually and update it as needed.\\n6. Keep it readily available to employees, their representatives, and OSHA on request.\\n7. Designate a competent person to make frequent and regular inspections of job sites, materials and equipment to carry out the plan.\\n\\n- If you cannot follow Table 1 exactly, you must assess exposure instead.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-23-t2\",\"ms\":11207,\"usd\":0.032,\"text\":\"The rest of the overhead line rules, beyond the distances already given: Table A has six voltage rows, and before you work inside them the rule asks for a planning meeting, a warning line, and a proximity alarm or dedicated spotter (29 CFR 1926.1408).\\n\\nTable A minimum clearance (nominal kV, AC) [10]:\\n- Up to 50 kV: 10 ft\\n- Over 50 to 200 kV: 15 ft\\n- Over 200 to 350 kV: 20 ft\\n- Over 350 to 500 kV: 25 ft\\n- Over 500 to 750 kV: 35 ft\\n- Over 750 to 1,000 kV: 45 ft\\n- Over 1,000 kV: the utility owner/operator or a registered professional engineer sets it.\\n\\nWhat must be in place when you work inside the 20 ft zone or the Table A distance [9]:\\n1. Hold a planning meeting with the operator and everyone near the machine or load to review where the lines are and how you will prevent contact.\\n2. Use non-conductive tag lines if tag lines are used.\\n3. Put up an elevated warning line, barricade or line of signs with flags, in the operator's view, at 20 ft (Option 2) or at the Table A distance (Option 3).\\n4. If the operator can't see that warning line, add a dedicated spotter on top of one of the other measures.\\n5. Use at least one of these: a proximity alarm set to warn early enough, or a dedicated spotter in continuous contact with the operator.\\n6. The spotter needs a visual aid for the clearance distance (a painted line, a line of stanchions, or line-of-sight landmarks) and must stand where they can judge the distance.\\n\\nOther rules to know:\\n- Nothing (equipment, load line, load or rigging) goes below a line unless the utility has deenergized and visibly grounded it. There are limited exceptions [2].\\n- The utility must give you voltage information within two working days of your request [2].\\n- Lines are presumed energized and uninsulated unless the utility or a registered engineer confirms otherwise [4].\\n- Operators and crew must be trained on contact procedures: stay in the cab unless there is fire or explosion, and know step potential and the safest way to evacuate. Dedicated spotters must be trained too [4].\\n- Alarms and similar devices must be used per the manufacturer's procedures [6].\\n- Subpart CC does not cover excavators working as excavators. Excavators doing excavation work are held to the 1926.600(a)(6) distance of 10 ft for lines up to 50 kV. Many crews use the Subpart CC distances anyway [5][11].\\n- In transit with the boom lowered, 1926.600(a)(6) allows 4 ft below 50 kV and 10 ft from 50 to 345 kV [11].\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-25-t2\",\"ms\":10810,\"usd\":0.0347,\"text\":\"Taper length for a 12 ft lane is L = W x S x S / 60 at 40 mph or less and W x S at 45 mph or more, from the national MUTCD (Arizona's supplement doesn't change it) [1]. The figures below are national MUTCD arithmetic, not an approved plan.\\n\\n1. At 35 mph: taper is 245 ft, with cones no more than 35 ft apart, which is 8 cones [10].\\n2. At 45 mph: taper is 540 ft, with cones 45 ft apart in the taper and 90 ft along the work, which is 13 cones [9][10].\\n3. Cone spacing is no more than 1 times the speed limit in feet in a taper and 2 times along the work. At 25 mph that is 25 ft and 50 ft; at 55 mph, 55 ft and 110 ft [9].\\n4. Buffer space, kept empty: 250 ft at 35 mph and 360 ft at 45 mph [10].\\n5. Downstream taper: 50 to 100 ft, with cones about 20 ft apart. The one-lane two-way taper in front of a flagger also uses cones about 20 ft apart [9][10].\\n6. Advance signs: three, with ROAD WORK AHEAD or UTILITY WORK AHEAD first, then lane closed, then lane ends. They are at least 100 ft apart on urban low speed streets and 350 ft apart on urban high speed streets [10].\\n7. Night: cones at least 28 inches tall with reflective bands. Tighter spacing is common at night and on curves [9][10].\\n\\n- The approved traffic control plan and the permit govern.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-01-t1\",\"ms\":4550,\"usd\":0.0771,\"text\":\"OSHA's Table B-1 allows a maximum slope of 1:1 (45°) in Type B soil for excavations less than 20 ft deep (29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B), so a 10 ft cut needs the top at least 10 ft back each side.\\n- Instead of sloping: benching (cohesive Type B only, 4 ft max per bench), shoring, or a trench box/shield.\\n- At 20 ft or deeper, a registered professional engineer must design it.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: bench dimensions and shield rules?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-02-t1\",\"ms\":4655,\"usd\":0.0772,\"text\":\"No. OSHA's Appendix B Type C configurations (B-1.3) list only simple slope (1 1/2:1 max) and a shielded/supported vertical lower portion with slope above, with no benching option (Texas follows federal OSHA).\\n- Any other Type C design must follow another § 1926.652(b) option, such as an engineered design.\\n- Employees can't work on sloped or benched faces above others unless protected (1926.652(f)).\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: the Type C slope options with a vertical lower portion?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-03-t1\",\"ms\":5802,\"usd\":0.0794,\"text\":\"Timber shoring at 10 ft in Type B is sized from the Appendix C tables: after you classify the soil under Appendix A, you pick crossbrace, wale and sheeting sizes and spacing by trench depth and width (29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, App. C). Federal OSHA is Ohio's rule here.\\n- App. C covers trenches that \\\"do not exceed 20 feet (6.1 m) in depth\\\", so 10 ft is within it.\\n- Other timber layouts must be designed under 1926.652(c).\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: how to read the Appendix C tables?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-04-t1\",\"ms\":6992,\"usd\":0.0785,\"text\":\"Federal OSHA, which is Colorado's rule for private crews, requires a protective system at 5 ft or deeper, and aluminum hydraulic shoring must be installed within the manufacturer's tabulated data for Type C soil (29 CFR 1926.652(c)(2)).\\n1. Get the manufacturer's tabulated data for your shores, and keep it at the jobsite.\\n2. Have the competent person classify the soil (Appendix A) before choosing the spacing.\\n3. Set the rails, shores and spacing exactly as the data shows for 8 ft in Type C.\\n4. Don't deviate without the manufacturer's written approval.\\n5. If you have no manufacturer's data, design it from Appendix D (trenches up to 20 ft).\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: Appendix D design steps and the rules for working inside the shoring?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-05-t1\",\"ms\":6100,\"usd\":0.0741,\"text\":\"Use the MUTCD TA-10 flagger setup: a flagger at each end, with advance signs in both directions (Oklahoma's state manual and your traffic control plan or permit govern).\\n1. Sign in the direction of travel, farthest upstream first: ROAD WORK AHEAD (or UTILITY WORK AHEAD), ONE LANE ROAD AHEAD, then the Flagger sign.\\n2. Set a one-lane two-way taper of 50 to 100 ft with cones about 20 ft apart.\\n3. Leave a buffer if there's room, and put cones along the work at no more than 2 times the speed limit in feet.\\n4. Add a downstream taper, light flagger stations at night, and take it all down in reverse.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\nWant the rest: sign spacing distances A, B and C for 45 mph?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-06-t1\",\"ms\":6182,\"usd\":0.0763,\"text\":\"At 55 mph the MUTCD sign spacing table puts you in the high-speed rows: 500 ft between signs on a rural road, or 1,000 / 1,500 / 2,640 ft on an expressway or freeway (MUTCD Part 6). [6]\\n- The road agency sets the speed category; the approved traffic control plan or permit governs.\\n- Arkansas's own sign spacing table is not confirmed in the library; ask ARDOT's traffic office which MUTCD edition is in force. [1]\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: taper length and cone spacing at 55 mph?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-07-t1\",\"ms\":4976,\"usd\":0.0768,\"text\":\"The merging taper for a 12 ft lane at 40 mph is at least 320 ft, from L = W x S x S / 60 (MUTCD Table 6B-4) [2][4].\\n- At 45 mph and up the formula changes to L = W x S, so the taper jumps to 540 ft.\\n- Your state manual and the approved traffic control plan or permit govern; round up if they say so.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-08-t1\",\"ms\":5690,\"usd\":0.0187,\"text\":\"You must give pedestrians a reasonably safe, accessible temporary walkway or detour, with advance signing so no one walks up to a closed sidewalk (MUTCD Part 6, Section 6C.02; federal OSHA 1926.200(g)(2) requires Part 6). Minnesota's own manual and your approved traffic control plan or permit govern, so follow whichever is stricter.\\n1. Post SIDEWALK CLOSED AHEAD CROSS HERE at the crossing before the closure, and SIDEWALK CLOSED at the closure.\\n2. Span the full closed width with a continuous barrier a cane can detect, not cones, tape or rope.\\n3. Keep the temporary route detectable, 60 inches wide where practical (48 inches with passing areas), with ramps 12:1 or flatter.\\n4. Cover or fence the open trench next to the walkway.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: ramp, edging and passing-area numbers for the temporary route?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-09-t1\",\"ms\":6612,\"usd\":0.0954,\"text\":\"Put each flagger station 250 ft ahead of the work space (35 mph stopping sight distance, MUTCD Table 6B-2), with advance warning signs ahead of it and lighting at night.\\n- Signs, in order from the approaching driver: ROAD WORK AHEAD, FLAGGER symbol sign (W20-7), ONE LANE ROAD AHEAD; BE PREPARED TO STOP goes between the last two.\\n- Add distance on a downgrade, and flaggers must hold an NCDOT-approved flagger course; the approved traffic control plan governs.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: sign spacing and taper length for your road?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-10-t1\",\"ms\":7035,\"usd\":0.0781,\"text\":\"Under 29 CFR 1926.1204(j), your permit program must cover preparing, issuing, using and canceling entry permits, and the entry supervisor authorizes entry by signing.\\n1. Isolate the space and control its hazards: lockout/tagging, purging, ventilating, flushing (1926.1206(i)).\\n2. Test the atmosphere and record results with the tester's name or initials and the time (1926.1206(k)).\\n3. List the hazards, the acceptable entry conditions, and a way to detect rising gas if ventilation stops (1926.1206(e), (h), (j)).\\n4. Name each attendant and the entry supervisor on the permit (1926.1206(f), (g)).\\n5. Set up rescue and emergency call procedures before anyone enters (1926.1204(i)).\\n6. The entry supervisor signs or initials to authorize entry, and the permit is canceled when the job ends.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: the gas limits (O2, LEL, H2S, CO) to test for?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-11-t1\",\"ms\":6382,\"usd\":0.0204,\"text\":\"Under 29 CFR 1926.1206 the entry permit must identify these items (Georgia follows the federal construction rule, so the same list applies):\\n1. The space, the purpose of entry, and the date with authorized duration.\\n2. Entrants (by name or roster), each attendant by name, and the entry supervisor with signature or initials.\\n3. Hazards of the space, isolation and control measures, and acceptable entry conditions.\\n4. Test results with tester's name or initials and when tested.\\n5. Rescue and emergency services and how to summon them, plus communication procedures.\\n6. Equipment (PPE, testing, alarms, rescue), how a rise in air hazard is detected if ventilation stops, and other needed safety information or permits such as hot work.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: how long to keep permits and who signs when?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-12-t1\",\"ms\":8976,\"usd\":0.0355,\"text\":\"Test oxygen first, then flammable gas, then toxic gases (H2S, CO), with a calibrated, bump-tested meter from outside, at top, middle and bottom (1926.1204(e)).\\n- Oxygen: below 19.5% is deficient, above 23.5% is enriched.\\n- Flammable gas: above 10% of the LFL/LEL is hazardous.\\n- Toxics: H2S 10 ppm (8-hour average). CO is 50 ppm federal and 25 ppm in the app's permit; use the lower.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: continuous monitoring and sewer entry rules?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-13-t1\",\"ms\":6464,\"usd\":0.0761,\"text\":\"Rescue must be arranged before anyone enters, and relying on 911 alone is not a plan (29 CFR 1926.1211(a)).\\n1. Call the responding fire department or rescue team first; confirm they do vertical manhole rescue and their response time, then write it on the permit.\\n2. Tell them the hazards and give them access for a practice rescue.\\n3. Put each entrant in a full-body harness with the retrieval line attached, and the other end fixed outside.\\n4. Set a tripod and winch over the manhole, since vertical spaces deeper than 5 ft require one.\\n5. Post an attendant outside who stays out and does non-entry rescue only.\\n6. Keep the address and nearest cross street ready for the EMERGENCY button script.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: attendant duties and the rescue team's evaluation?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-14-t1\",\"ms\":5661,\"usd\":0.0939,\"text\":\"In Nevada, call USA North 811 for a Renewal ticket before day 28 ends, because a ticket is good for 28 calendar days (NAC 455.165).\\n1. Renew only if the marks are still clear; if they're gone, request a Re-Mark.\\n2. You get two 28-day extensions at most, 84 days on one ticket.\\n3. After that, open a new ticket (2 working days' wait); call it in 2 working days before the last renewal expires so there's no gap.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-15-t1\",\"ms\":5419,\"usd\":0.0947,\"text\":\"Refresh the ticket now by calling 811 or using the Texas811 portal for an Update (Update and Remark) covering only the area still to dig; it goes out with a 2 business day notice (Tex. Util. Code ch. 251 / 16 TAC 18.3) [1][3].\\n\\n1. Don't dig in the uncovered area until the update is in and the operators respond [3][4].\\n2. Request it early: if the latest ticket is over 30 days old, you need a new ticket [3].\\n3. Wait for each operator's positive response; with none, give a second notice, and after 4 hours with none you may begin [3].\\n4. Enter the new ticket or date in the app's Locates screen [6].\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-16-t1\",\"ms\":8240,\"usd\":0.0188,\"text\":\"Bed PVC sewer on a uniform, even layer of crushed stone or the spec'd bedding, then haunch and compact the sides, because for flexible pipe the sidefill carries the load (ASTM D2321).\\n\\n1. Check the trench bottom; if it is soft, wet or rock, build a foundation first [5].\\n2. Place and shape the bedding so the pipe sits evenly supported along its full length [5].\\n3. Lay the pipe, then work material under the curve up to the springline; this zone matters most [5].\\n4. Compact the haunches and sides, since sidefill compaction controls performance [2].\\n5. Fill to at least 6 inches over the crown, often 12 inches by spec, then final backfill [5].\\n\\nNevada's library has Clark County's standard of at least 4 in of bedding, with the pipe zone in Type II aggregate base compacted to 90 percent [1]. Reno's own spec isn't in the library; check it.\\n\\nWant the rest: crushed stone versus rounded gravel for the pipe zone?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-17-t1\",\"ms\":5327,\"usd\":0.0173,\"text\":\"Pressure test the new PVC main (AWWA C605) at your spec's pressure, commonly 1.5 times working pressure or 150 psi minimum, for at least 2 hours, with make-up water within L = S x D x sqrt(P) / 148,000 gal/hr [3].\\n\\n1. Install thrust restraint first, then fill slowly and bleed all air at hydrants, air valves and taps [5][3].\\n2. Connect the test pump and a calibrated gauge, with a measured make-up water source [6].\\n3. Raise to test pressure and hold, pumping in make-up water to keep it [3].\\n4. Compare the measured make-up water to the allowable; 1,000 ft of 8 in at 150 psi allows about 0.66 gal/hr [3].\\n5. Pressure that keeps dropping usually means air, a passing valve, or a leaking joint or tap [3].\\n- Keep people away from plugs, caps and thrust blocks under pressure, and never tighten joints under pressure [6].\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: allowable leakage per 1,000 ft by pipe size?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-18-t1\",\"ms\":6286,\"usd\":0.0172,\"text\":\"Disinfect it under AWWA C651 in this order, using the method your spec names (the agency spec governs).\\n1. Keep pipe clean while laying: plugs on open ends, no trench water in the pipe.\\n2. Fill slowly through a backflow-protected connection with 25 mg/L chlorine (tablet or continuous feed) and hold 24 hours.\\n3. Confirm at least 10 mg/L (continuous feed) at the end, then flush to system chlorine levels.\\n4. Dechlorinate the flush water before it reaches a drain or stream.\\n5. Take bac-T samples; connect only after they pass.\\n- Slug method instead: 100 mg/L for at least 3 hours.\\n\\nWant the rest: tablet method fill rate, cold-water hold time and sample timing?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-19-t1\",\"ms\":6215,\"usd\":0.0182,\"text\":\"California's heat rule (8 CCR 3395) requires water, shade, cool-down rests, acclimatization and a written plan on every outdoor job, trench crews included, and it is stricter than federal OSHA's general guidance.\\n1. Provide fresh, cool water close to the work, at least 1 quart per worker per hour for the whole shift.\\n2. Keep shade up when it's over 80 F, big enough for everyone on a break.\\n3. Let anyone take a cool-down rest in the shade, at least 5 minutes.\\n4. Watch new and returning workers closely for their first 14 days.\\n5. At 95 F and above, run high-heat procedures.\\n6. Keep a written Heat Illness Prevention Plan and emergency response plan at the site.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: the high-heat procedures at 95 F and above?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-20-t1\",\"ms\":4641,\"usd\":0.0208,\"text\":\"OSHA requires a trench box (shield) at 12 ft to be a manufactured or engineer-designed system that resists all loads it could see (29 CFR 1926.652).\\n\\n1. Get the soil type from a competent person first. Appendix A classification is required before using any tabulated data.\\n2. Use the manufacturer's tabulated data or an engineer-approved design. Match the box's rated depth and soil type to your 12 ft cut.\\n3. Tennessee's OSHA plan can be stricter, so confirm with Tennessee's OSHA plan.\\n4. Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: how Appendix D tables size aluminum hydraulic shoring?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-21-t1\",\"ms\":6442,\"usd\":0.0227,\"text\":\"Federal OSHA is Florida's rule for private crews, and at 6 ft it requires a protective system (sloping, benching, shoring or a trench box) unless the trench is entirely in stable rock (29 CFR 1926.652(a)(1)).\\n1. Exit: a ladder or other way out within 25 ft of lateral travel, since the trench is 4 ft or deeper.\\n2. Spoil and equipment: keep at least 2 ft from the edge.\\n3. Air testing: required where a hazardous atmosphere could exist.\\n4. Inspection: the competent person inspects daily and after rain.\\n5. Slopes: Type A 3/4:1, Type B 1:1, Type C 1 1/2:1.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: shield rules and sloping surcharge requirements?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-22-t1\",\"ms\":5535,\"usd\":0.0202,\"text\":\"Table 1 of the silica rule (29 CFR 1926.1153(c)) requires a saw with an integrated water feed that runs continuously to the blade, so no dry cutting.\\n\\n1. Use a saw with built-in water delivery, with water at a flow that minimizes visible dust.\\n2. Wear an APF 10 respirator if you cut more than 4 hours a shift outdoors, or at any time indoors or in an enclosed area.\\n3. Follow the written exposure control plan and keep no dry sweeping or compressed air cleanup.\\n\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: the stationary saw, walk-behind saw and written plan details?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-23-t1\",\"ms\":3973,\"usd\":0.02,\"text\":\"Keep at least 20 feet from the line unless the utility confirms the voltage, then the Table A distance applies: 10 ft up to 50 kV, 15 ft over 50 to 200 kV (29 CFR 1926.1408).\\n\\n- Treat every line as energized unless the utility says it is deenergized and visibly grounded.\\n- Use a dedicated spotter and a warning line or proximity alarm.\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-24-t1\",\"ms\":10103,\"usd\":0.029,\"text\":\"Colorado issues its own construction stormwater permit, and the library doesn't hold it, so follow the SWPPP and permit your company has on file (check with CDPHE Water Quality). EPA's permit gives the baseline: a SWPPP kept on site, routine inspections, and fixes on a clock (Colorado's permit may be stricter). [1][9]\\n\\n1. Keep a current SWPPP at the site, with the dates of every change (EPA CGP Part 7.3, 7.4.2). [2]\\n2. A qualified person inspects every 7 days, or every 14 days plus within 24 hours of a 0.25 inch rain (Part 4.2). [6]\\n3. Fix controls: routine maintenance by the close of the next business day; new or significant repairs within 7 days (Part 5.2.1). [6]\\n4. Clean sediment out of silt fence and wattles before it reaches half the height (Part 2.2.3). [3]\\n5. Stabilize idle ground within 14 calendar days; wash concrete only into a leak-proof container or lined pit (Parts 2.2.14, 2.3.4). [3]\\n6. Keep inspection reports and the corrective action log on site, and for 3 years after coverage ends (Parts 4.7.4, 5.4.4). [2]\\n\\nWant the rest: which Colorado permit terms to check against these numbers?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-25-t1\",\"ms\":6591,\"usd\":0.0198,\"text\":\"Night work in Arizona runs on the approved traffic control plan and the permit, with the national MUTCD Part 6 setting the details (Arizona's supplement doesn't change tapers, sign spacing or flagger rules) [1]. Setup steps:\\n1. Get the approved traffic control plan and the agency's night-work conditions [1][8].\\n2. Set signs in the direction of traffic, starting with the farthest advance sign, then the taper, then the channelizing along the work [5].\\n3. Use retroreflective or lit signs and devices, with cones at least 28 inches tall with white bands [4].\\n4. Light every flagger station, and aim floodlights so they don't glare at drivers [4].\\n5. Dress all workers in Class 2 or 3 apparel, with flaggers in Class 3 at night [2].\\n6. Drive through from each direction after setup and again during the night, then remove devices in reverse order [4][5].\\n\\n- Your competent person decides on site.\\n\\nWant the rest: taper length and cone spacing figures?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-26-t1\",\"ms\":8019,\"usd\":0.0254,\"text\":\"Block bearing area = thrust ÷ allowable soil bearing, and for a 90 degree bend the thrust is T = 0.50 x pi x P x d² x sin(45°) (VCMWD standard) [7][2].\\n\\n- Example only: 8 inch C900 (OD 9.05 in) at 150 psi test pressure gives about 13,646 lb thrust. In sand at about 4,000 lb/sq ft, that is about 3.4 sq ft of bearing area [7][2].\\n- Use the actual test pressure, pipe OD and soil value. Pour against undisturbed soil, and build what the plans or agency detail shows [2][7].\\n\\nWant the rest: restrained joints instead of blocks?\",\"status\":200},{\"id\":\"fu7-27-t1\",\"ms\":5956,\"usd\":0.0216,\"text\":\"Under federal OSHA (which is Oklahoma's rule for private crews), the competent person must inspect the excavation, adjacent areas and protective systems daily and pull workers out when a hazard shows up (29 CFR 1926.651(k)).\\n1. Inspect before work starts, as needed through the shift, and after every rainstorm or other hazard-increasing event.\\n2.
